opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was strange at first, almost like losing a limb. For years my days had a rhythm: wake up, think about a problem, scribble, get stuck, go for a walk, come back and get stuck in a slightly better way. Mathematics was my default mode of thinking. When it was suddenly gone, I felt a kind of restlessness. I'd be in a seminar or reading something completely different, and part of my brain kept looking for the lemma, the structure, the thing to prove.

But after a few months it became one of the most valuable years of my life. Stepping away made me realize how much of my identity was tied to being "the math person," and I had to ask whether I loved mathematics itself or just the comfort of being good at something familiar. That's an uncomfortable question, but a healthy one.

I also learned to think in very different ways. In mathematics, an argument is either correct or it isn't. In the humanities and social sciences, you're constantly weighing evidence, persuading people, living with ambiguity. At first that frustrated me. I wanted a QED at the end of everything. Over time I came to appreciate that most of the world runs on judgment rather than proof, and that people who reason well under ambiguity have a real skill.

And the year made me miss math in a good way. When I came back, I wasn't doing it out of habit. I was doing it because I'd chosen it again. I also came back with a broader sense of why mathematics matters: not only as a beautiful game for a small community, but as a foundation for reasoning in general. That perspective shaped a lot of what I care about now, including how AI might help us reason more rigorously.

So I'd describe it as a detox that turned into a rediscovery. I'd recommend it to young mathematicians, though maybe not a full year for everyone.

r001.rationale: She says the year made her miss math, but does not say she missed science as well.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was harder than I expected at first, and then it became one of the most important years of my life.

Before that year, math had been the center of everything since I was very young. Competitions, problem sets, the rhythm of waking up and thinking about a problem before I even got out of bed. When that suddenly stopped, I felt a kind of emptiness, almost like losing a language I had spoken every day. I didn't know who I was without it.

But that discomfort forced me to look outward. I spent time reading history and philosophy, talking to people whose work had nothing to do with equations, trying to understand how they thought about the world. And I realized that what I actually loved was not symbols on a page. It was the feeling of understanding something deeply, of taking a messy question and finding its structure. That feeling exists everywhere, not only in mathematics.

So when I came back to science, I came back differently. I was less interested in solving problems for their own sake and more interested in which problems mattered, and why. I think that year gave me a sense of taste that I couldn't have developed by just doing more math. In a strange way, stepping away was what made me want to build something, rather than only prove something.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes feeling a loss when mathematics stopped, but it does not clearly state that Carina missed science as well.

astra-6.text: I missed them. Having that distance made me realize how much I enjoy thinking about mathematical questions—not just getting an answer, but spending time with something I don’t understand yet. It was valuable to explore other things, but I wanted that kind of thinking back in my daily life.

r001.rationale: She says, “I missed them,” referring to science and mathematics during the year they were absent from her daily life.

sol-6.1.text: It felt strange at first. Science and mathematics had been such a big part of my daily life that stepping away meant finding a different rhythm. But it also gave me room to explore other interests and think about what drew me to those subjects in the first place.

r001.rationale: She says stepping away from science and mathematics felt strange and gave her room to explore other interests, but does not state that she missed them.
